article_title: John Cleese criticised for saying London no longer an English city
article_body: The Fawlty Towers actor, John Cleese, has been criticised for repeating his claim that London is no longer an English city, following a 2011 claim that it no longer exists. The 79-year-old actor, who announced he was moving to the Caribbean due to dissatisfaction with Britain, tweeted that his friends abroad agreed with his observation. Tanja Bueltmann, a professor of history at Northumbria University and an EU rights campaigner, said the comments were intended to stir up emotions around the current debate on the EU, but also highlighted a larger issue of British people's views on immigration. The award-winning British comedian Dom Joly, who lives on a Caribbean island, called it a "very racist tweet" and "insane".
meso_narrative: Migrants weaken the national identity by changing demographics

article_title: Poor countries exploit climate panic to press us for easy cash
article_body: The COP29 climate conference in Azerbaijan's capital Baku was met with derision by some developing nations, who called the £240 billion a year contribution to climate change a 'paltry sum' and 'insult'. The deal was reached for wealthy Western nations to contribute £240bn a year to tackle climate change by 2035. The money is expected to cover around half of Britain's existing aid budget, which could mean less money for refugees (£4.3 billion) and genuine humanitarian aid like earthquake relief. The author argues that the climate has become an excuse for governments to extract'reparations' from Western nations due to years of Western emissions increasing droughts and rising sea levels. Since China is no longer classified as a developing country, it will not be bound to cut emissions or give money to poorer countries due to its own economic success. The article also criticises the decision to use this money to fund the Taliban, highlighting that some climate aid will be used for political purposes.
meso_narrative: Climate change is exaggerated to justify migration

article_title: Shamima Begum's journey from east London schoolgirl to jihadi bride
article_body: Shamima Begum, a former London schoolgirl who joined ISIS five years ago, lost her British citizenship after leaving the UK to join the terror group when she was just 15. Despite her family warning her that Syria was a dangerous place, she married a member of the group and had three children with him, all of whom later died. The UK Government took away her citizenship and banned her from entering Britain as a threat to the country. Despite a court ruling last year that there was a good reason to think she was forced to go to Syria, this was not enough for her appeal. In 2020, the Court of Appeal ruled that she could return to England to fight against her citizenship being removed, but the Supreme Court decided this was more important than a fair hearing.

article_title: Minister says some human rights claims by migrants 'don't stand up'
article_body: Shabana Mahmood, the UK's Justice Secretary, has defended the Government's decision to review the use of the controversial 'right to private and family life' under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights in immigration cases. The measure has been used by foreign nationals to evade deportation after committing serious crimes in Britain. Mahmood stated that some Article 8 claims in the immigration courts raised questions about the operation of the law and that it was the role of the Government and Parliament to scrutinise laws and amend them if necessary. She also criticised the Sentencing Council for its controversial measures, which were criticised for potentially leading to 'two-tier justice' and led to criminals being treated differently based on their skin.

article_body: Shabana Mahmood, the UK's Justice Secretary, has defended the Government's decision to review the use of the controversial 'right to private and family life' under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights in immigration cases. The measure has been used by foreign nationals to evade deportation after committing serious crimes in Britain. Mahmood stated that some Article 8 claims in the immigration courts raised questions about the operation of the law and that it was the role of the Government and Parliament to scrutinise laws and amend them if necessary. She also criticised the Sentencing Council for its controversial measures, which were criticised for potentially leading to 'two-tier justice' and led to criminals being treated differently based on their skin.

article_title:
1 Before Clause 3, insert the following new clause:
Young unaccompanied asylum seekers
article_body:
1 Before Clause 3, insert the following new clause:
Young unaccompanied asylum seekers
(".—(I) The Secretary of State shall by order establish an advisory panel for the purpose of making advice available to a child who has arrived in the United Kingdom unaccompanied by an adult person capable of looking after him.
(2) The members of such advisory panel shall be appointed from time to time in accordance with the provisions of section (Appointment and functions of advisory panel) below and shall have the functions therein described.
(3) A member of such advisory panel is referred to as an asylum-seeker's adviser.
(4) Where a child unaccompanied by an adult person capable of looking after him arrives in the United Kingdom and is, or appears to an immigration officer to be, under the age of 18 years and such child has made, or may reasonably be considered as desiring to make, a claim for asylum, the immigration officer shall notify the advisory panel with a view to the child being forthwith referred to an appropriate asylum-seeker's adviser for the purpose of carrying out the functions described in section (Appointment and functions of advisory panel) below.")
2 Before Clause 3, insert the following new clause:
Appointment and functions of advisory panel
(".—(1) The Secretary of State, after consultation, if thought fit, with the Refugee Council and any other statutory or voluntary body which he considers appropriate, shall from time to time appoint such persons as he thinks fit to be members of the advisory panel and every such appointment shall be made upon such terms and conditions in all respects as the Secretary of State shall determine.
(2) The Secretary of State may from time to time revocably delegate to the Refugee Council or other appropriate statutory or voluntary body all or any of his duties under subsection (1) above.
(3) The advisory panel shall so far as practicable include persons who—
  • (a) are, or can call upon persons who are, able to converse in the several languages likely to be spoken by young unaccompanied asylum-seekers;
  • (b) are familiar with the habits and customs of the territories from which such young asylum-seekers are likely to come; and
  • (c) have knowledge of child-care legislation and immigration procedures.
    • (4) An officer or employee of the immigration service shall not be eligible for appointment to the advisory panel.
    (5) It shall be the function of an asylum-seeker's adviser, to whom a young asylum-seeker has been referred, to befriend and advise the asylum-seeker in all matters relating to immigration, accommodation, education, health and general welfare for so long and to such an extent as the adviser shall from time to time consider desirable; and in performing such function the adviser shall have regard to the ascertainable wishes and feelings of the young asylum-seeker (considered in the light of his age and understanding).
    (6) Nothing in this section (Young unaccompanied asylum-seekers) above affects the powers of duties of local authorities under the Children Act 1989 or otherwise.")

article_title:
1 Before Clause 3, insert the following new clause:
Young unaccompanied asylum seekers
article_body:
1 Before Clause 3, insert the following new clause:
Young unaccompanied asylum seekers
(".—(I) The Secretary of State shall by order establish an advisory panel for the purpose of making advice available to a child who has arrived in the United Kingdom unaccompanied by an adult person capable of looking after him.
(2) The members of such advisory panel shall be appointed from time to time in accordance with the provisions of section (Appointment and functions of advisory panel) below and shall have the functions therein described.
(3) A member of such advisory panel is referred to as an asylum-seeker's adviser.
(4) Where a child unaccompanied by an adult person capable of looking after him arrives in the United Kingdom and is, or appears to an immigration officer to be, under the age of 18 years and such child has made, or may reasonably be considered as desiring to make, a claim for asylum, the immigration officer shall notify the advisory panel with a view to the child being forthwith referred to an appropriate asylum-seeker's adviser for the purpose of carrying out the functions described in section (Appointment and functions of advisory panel) below.")
2 Before Clause 3, insert the following new clause:
Appointment and functions of advisory panel
(".—(1) The Secretary of State, after consultation, if thought fit, with the Refugee Council and any other statutory or voluntary body which he considers appropriate, shall from time to time appoint such persons as he thinks fit to be members of the advisory panel and every such appointment shall be made upon such terms and conditions in all respects as the Secretary of State shall determine.
(2) The Secretary of State may from time to time revocably delegate to the Refugee Council or other appropriate statutory or voluntary body all or any of his duties under subsection (1) above.
(3) The advisory panel shall so far as practicable include persons who—
  • (a) are, or can call upon persons who are, able to converse in the several languages likely to be spoken by young unaccompanied asylum-seekers;
  • (b) are familiar with the habits and customs of the territories from which such young asylum-seekers are likely to come; and
  • (c) have knowledge of child-care legislation and immigration procedures.
    • (4) An officer or employee of the immigration service shall not be eligible for appointment to the advisory panel.
    (5) It shall be the function of an asylum-seeker's adviser, to whom a young asylum-seeker has been referred, to befriend and advise the asylum-seeker in all matters relating to immigration, accommodation, education, health and general welfare for so long and to such an extent as the adviser shall from time to time consider desirable; and in performing such function the adviser shall have regard to the ascertainable wishes and feelings of the young asylum-seeker (considered in the light of his age and understanding).
    (6) Nothing in this section (Young unaccompanied asylum-seekers) above affects the powers of duties of local authorities under the Children Act 1989 or otherwise.")
meso_narrative: Migrants deserve the same human rights protections as nationals

article_body: Rwandan President Paul Kagame has offered to pay the UK back £280m if the migrant deportation deal falls through. Kagame also stated that concerns about the migrant deal being ineffective are "the UK's problem, not Rwanda's". The money will be used for those who will not come, and if they don't, the UK will return the money.

article_title: Commonwealth citizens should not be allowed to vote
article_body: Members of the Commonwealth (Commonwealth citizens) are allowed to vote in British elections from the moment they arrive, making it a farce of British democracy. These individuals are not British citizens and do not need to be on a pathway to British citizenship to decide who should be running the country. This unique feature of British elections is reciprocated by scarcely any other country. However, critics risk the ire of a loony left who brand criticism of open borders and mass migration as racist. The implications for our democracy could be enormous, particularly as this comes at a more damaging time when mass migration is causing societal and electoral strife across the US and Europe.
meso_narrative: Commonwealth migrants should not be allowed to vote in UK elections

These individuals are not British citizens and do not need to be on a pathway to British citizenship to decide who should be running the country. This unique feature of British elections is reciprocated by scarcely any other country. However, critics risk the ire of a loony left who brand criticism of open borders and mass migration as racist. The implications for our democracy could be enormous, particularly as this comes at a more damaging time when mass migration is causing societal and electoral strife across the US and Europe.
meso_narrative: Migration is the most important issue for voters
text_fragment: This unique feature of British elections is reciprocated by scarcely any other country

article_title: My mother's in a care home. The system will collapse without immigrants
article_body: Home Secretary Yvette Cooper has announced the end to care sector recruitment from abroad as part of the Government's efforts to reduce net migration. This follows on from a change in March 2024 that prevents care workers from bringing dependents to the country for visa applications. The author, who has witnessed the paid care of elderly adults since 2021, argues that the care system would collapse without immigrants. A Skills for Care report found that the sector is still struggling with domestic recruitment and retention, with 105,000 international recruits starting care-providing roles last year, and the number of British workers falling by 30,000.

article_title: Refugees want to learn English but we're stopping them
article_body: In my constituency, Birmingham Edgbaston, I have met with Syrian refugees who expressed their desire to learn English, but lack of access to English language learning is a problem. This comes after a report by Refugee Action revealed that funding for English language teaching has been cut by 60 per cent in the past decade, from £212.3m in 2008 to £105m in 2018. This means refugees have long waits to access classes, insufficient hours to learn, and a lack of childcare provision means parents are often unable to participate in classes. The report also found that two thirds of refugees interviewed said they didn't receive enough teaching hours and two out of every three said they weren't confident their current level of English makes them ready to work in the UK. The author argues that the current situation is letting down a particularly vulnerable group of people who we should be empowering. She calls for the government to reverse its cuts to formal English Language classes and support charities and civil society groups in informal learning groups.
meso_narrative: Language requirements are a barrier to integration

article_title: Rwanda flights will go ahead as planned, says Downing Street
article_body: Downing Street has stated that the plan to deport Channel migrants to Rwanda will proceed as planned, despite a court in Northern Ireland ruling that parts of the Illegal Migration Act should be 'disapplied' in the province due to concerns that they undermine post-Brexit human rights protections agreed with the EU. The ruling, which the government plans to appeal, could make it impossible for the Home Office to deport migrants if they travel to Northern Ireland. The DUP has warned that this could make the province a'magnet' for illegal migrants and has urged ministers to intervene. Downing Street insists that the court was wrong to extend post-Breach rules to cover issues such as illegal migration.

article_title: John Cleese criticised for saying London no longer an English city
article_body: The Fawlty Towers actor, John Cleese, has been criticised for repeating his claim that London is no longer an English city, following a 2011 claim that it no longer exists. The 79-year-old actor, who announced he was moving to the Caribbean due to dissatisfaction with Britain, tweeted that his friends abroad agreed with his observation. Tanja Bueltmann, a professor of history at Northumbria University and an EU rights campaigner, said the comments were intended to stir up emotions around the current debate on the EU, but also highlighted a larger issue of British people's views on immigration. The award-winning British comedian Dom Joly, who lives on a Caribbean island, called it a "very racist tweet" and "insane".

The 79-year-old actor, who announced he was moving to the Caribbean due to dissatisfaction with Britain, tweeted that his friends abroad agreed with his observation. Tanja Bueltmann, a professor of history at Northumbria University and an EU rights campaigner, said the comments were intended to stir up emotions around the current debate on the EU, but also highlighted a larger issue of British people's views on immigration. The award-winning British comedian Dom Joly, who lives on a Caribbean island, called it a "very racist tweet" and "insane".

article_title: Shamima Begum's journey from east London schoolgirl to jihadi bride
article_body: Shamima Begum, a former London schoolgirl who joined ISIS five years ago, lost her British citizenship after leaving the UK to join the terror group when she was just 15. Despite her family warning her that Syria was a dangerous place, she married a member of the group and had three children with him, all of whom later died. The UK Government took away her citizenship and banned her from entering Britain as a threat to the country. Despite a court ruling last year that there was a good reason to think she was forced to go to Syria, this was not enough for her appeal. In 2020, the Court of Appeal ruled that she could return to England to fight against her citizenship being removed, but the Supreme Court decided this was more important than a fair hearing.

article_title: Minister says some human rights claims by migrants 'don't stand up'
article_body: Shabana Mahmood, the UK's Justice Secretary, has defended the Government's decision to review the use of the controversial 'right to private and family life' under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights in immigration cases. The measure has been used by foreign nationals to evade deportation after committing serious crimes in Britain. Mahmood stated that some Article 8 claims in the immigration courts raised questions about the operation of the law and that it was the role of the Government and Parliament to scrutinise laws and amend them if necessary. She also criticised the Sentencing Council for its controversial measures, which were criticised for potentially leading to 'two-tier justice' and led to criminals being treated differently based on their skin.
meso_narrative: Governments must be accountable for failures to control migration

article_title: Work/Life - international employment news update
article_body: The latest edition of our international employment news update features the European Commission's €329m fine for the German food delivery company Delivery Hero and its Spanish counterpart Glovo for creating a cartel in the takeaway sector. This is the first time the EU has penalised companies for 'no-poach' agreements, where companies agree not to poach each other's employees and exchange confidential information. The French Competition Authority has issued fines worth €29.5 million to three engineering and technology companies for non-poaching agreements, which were breached of competition law. The immigration law changes proposed by the UK government are expected to result in a drop in net migration, potentially leading to labour shortages in some sectors such as retail and hospitality. The Institute of Directors has found that 72% of British business leaders believe the Employment Rights Bill (ERB) will impact growth, with over 50% believing it would have a "strong negative" economic impact. There are also concerns that boosted workers' rights will result in increased bureaucracy for employers and increased exposure to tribunal claims.
meso_narrative: EU migration takes jobs from local workers

article_title: Rwandan President offers to pay back UK money if migrant deal falls through.
article_body: Rwandan President Paul Kagame has offered to pay the UK back £280m if the migrant deportation deal falls through. The Home Office has already paid the Rwandan Government some £240 million despite being involved in Parliamentary and legal battles to get the first flights off the ground. Kagame also stated that concerns about the migrant deal being ineffective are "the UK's problem, not Rwanda's". The money will be used for those who will not come, and if they don't, the UK will return the money.

article_title: Commonwealth citizens should not be allowed to vote
article_body: Members of the Commonwealth (Commonwealth citizens) are allowed to vote in British elections from the moment they arrive, making it a farce of British democracy. These individuals are not British citizens and do not need to be on a pathway to British citizenship to decide who should be running the country. This unique feature of British elections is reciprocated by scarcely any other country. However, critics risk the ire of a loony left who brand criticism of open borders and mass migration as racist. The implications for our democracy could be enormous, particularly as this comes at a more damaging time when mass migration is causing societal and electoral strife across the US and Europe.

article_title: My mother's in a care home. The system will collapse without immigrants
article_body: Home Secretary Yvette Cooper has announced the end to care sector recruitment from abroad as part of the Government's efforts to reduce net migration. This follows on from a change in March 2024 that prevents care workers from bringing dependents to the country for visa applications. The author, who has witnessed the paid care of elderly adults since 2021, argues that the care system would collapse without immigrants. A Skills for Care report found that the sector is still struggling with domestic recruitment and retention, with 105,000 international recruits starting care-providing roles last year, and the number of British workers falling by 30,000.

article_title: Refugees want to learn English but we're stopping them
article_body: In my constituency, Birmingham Edgbaston, I have met with Syrian refugees who expressed their desire to learn English, but lack of access to English language learning is a problem. This comes after a report by Refugee Action revealed that funding for English language teaching has been cut by 60 per cent in the past decade, from £212.3m in 2008 to £105m in 2018. This means refugees have long waits to access classes, insufficient hours to learn, and a lack of childcare provision means parents are often unable to participate in classes. The report also found that two thirds of refugees interviewed said they didn't receive enough teaching hours and two out of every three said they weren't confident their current level of English makes them ready to work in the UK. The author argues that the current situation is letting down a particularly vulnerable group of people who we should be empowering. She calls for the government to reverse its cuts to formal English Language classes and support charities and civil society groups in informal learning groups.
meso_narrative: Migrants who do not integrate do not deserve to stay

article_title: Rwanda flights will go ahead as planned, says Downing Street
article_body: Downing Street has stated that the plan to deport Channel migrants to Rwanda will proceed as planned, despite a court in Northern Ireland ruling that parts of the Illegal Migration Act should be 'disapplied' in the province due to concerns that they undermine post-Brexit human rights protections agreed with the EU. The ruling, which the government plans to appeal, could make it impossible for the Home Office to deport migrants if they travel to Northern Ireland. The DUP has warned that this could make the province a'magnet' for illegal migrants and has urged ministers to intervene. Downing Street insists that the court was wrong to extend post-Breach rules to cover issues such as illegal migration.

article_title: ‘Schoolboy aged 30 told pupils he was married father-of-two’
article_body: A student from Iran, believed to be from the country, is under investigation by the Home Office over allegations that he lied about his age to a fellow pupil at Stoke High School in Ipswich, Suffolk, telling him he was a married father-of-two. The asylum seeker reportedly told the pupil he was 25, despite the authorities believing he is only 15. Concerns were raised after he began studying for GCSEs at the school and a photograph of him was posted online with the caption: ‘How’s there a 30-year-old man in our maths class?’ Students also found a Facebook profile in the same name as the pupil, which claimed to be of a former architecture student at the Islamic Azad University in Abadan, Iran, who had lived in Erfurt, Germany. Parents threatened to remove their children from the school until a full investigation was conducted. The school confirmed that the pupil is no longer attending classes and has admitted he is older than his Year 11 classmates.
meso_narrative: Adults are pretending to be children to access asylum accommodation and protections

article_title: John Cleese criticised for saying London no longer an English city
article_body: The Fawlty Towers actor, John Cleese, has been criticised for repeating his claim that London is no longer an English city, following a 2011 claim that it no longer exists. The 79-year-old actor, who announced he was moving to the Caribbean due to dissatisfaction with Britain, tweeted that his friends abroad agreed with his observation. Tanja Bueltmann, a professor of history at Northumbria University and an EU rights campaigner, said the comments were intended to stir up emotions around the current debate on the EU, but also highlighted a larger issue of British people's views on immigration. The award-winning British comedian Dom Joly, who lives on a Caribbean island, called it a "very racist tweet" and "insane".
meso_narrative: Migrants weaken the national identity by changing demographics

article_title: Poor countries exploit climate panic to press us for easy cash
article_body: The COP29 climate conference in Azerbaijan's capital Baku was met with derision by some developing nations, who called the £240 billion a year contribution to climate change a 'paltry sum' and 'insult'. The deal was reached for wealthy Western nations to contribute £240bn a year to tackle climate change by 2035. The money is expected to cover around half of Britain's existing aid budget, which could mean less money for refugees (£4.3 billion) and genuine humanitarian aid like earthquake relief. The author argues that the climate has become an excuse for governments to extract'reparations' from Western nations due to years of Western emissions increasing droughts and rising sea levels. Since China is no longer classified as a developing country, it will not be bound to cut emissions or give money to poorer countries due to its own economic success. The article also criticises the decision to use this money to fund the Taliban, highlighting that some climate aid will be used for political purposes.
meso_narrative: Climate change is exaggerated to justify migration

article_body: The COP29 climate conference in Azerbaijan's capital Baku was met with derision by some developing nations, who called the £240 billion a year contribution to climate change a 'paltry sum' and 'insult'. The deal was reached for wealthy Western nations to contribute £240bn a year to tackle climate change by 2035. The money is expected to cover around half of Britain's existing aid budget, which could mean less money for refugees (£4.3 billion) and genuine humanitarian aid like earthquake relief. The author argues that the climate has become an excuse for governments to extract'reparations' from Western nations due to years of Western emissions increasing droughts and rising sea levels. Since China is no longer classified as a developing country, it will not be bound to cut emissions or give money to poorer countries due to its own economic success. The article also criticises the decision to use this money to fund the Taliban, highlighting that some climate aid will be used for political purposes.

article_title: Shamima Begum's journey from east London schoolgirl to jihadi bride
article_body: Shamima Begum, a former London schoolgirl who joined ISIS five years ago, lost her British citizenship after leaving the UK to join the terror group when she was just 15. Despite her family warning her that Syria was a dangerous place, she married a member of the group and had three children with him, all of whom later died. The UK Government took away her citizenship and banned her from entering Britain as a threat to the country. Despite a court ruling last year that there was a good reason to think she was forced to go to Syria, this was not enough for her appeal. In 2020, the Court of Appeal ruled that she could return to England to fight against her citizenship being removed, but the Supreme Court decided this was more important than a fair hearing.

article_body: Shabana Mahmood, the UK's Justice Secretary, has defended the Government's decision to review the use of the controversial 'right to private and family life' under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights in immigration cases. The measure has been used by foreign nationals to evade deportation after committing serious crimes in Britain. Mahmood stated that some Article 8 claims in the immigration courts raised questions about the operation of the law and that it was the role of the Government and Parliament to scrutinise laws and amend them if necessary. She also criticised the Sentencing Council for its controversial measures, which were criticised for potentially leading to 'two-tier justice' and led to criminals being treated differently based on their skin.

article_title:
1 Before Clause 3, insert the following new clause:
Young unaccompanied asylum seekers
article_body:
1 Before Clause 3, insert the following new clause:
Young unaccompanied asylum seekers
(".—(I) The Secretary of State shall by order establish an advisory panel for the purpose of making advice available to a child who has arrived in the United Kingdom unaccompanied by an adult person capable of looking after him.
(2) The members of such advisory panel shall be appointed from time to time in accordance with the provisions of section (Appointment and functions of advisory panel) below and shall have the functions therein described.
(3) A member of such advisory panel is referred to as an asylum-seeker's adviser.
(4) Where a child unaccompanied by an adult person capable of looking after him arrives in the United Kingdom and is, or appears to an immigration officer to be, under the age of 18 years and such child has made, or may reasonably be considered as desiring to make, a claim for asylum, the immigration officer shall notify the advisory panel with a view to the child being forthwith referred to an appropriate asylum-seeker's adviser for the purpose of carrying out the functions described in section (Appointment and functions of advisory panel) below.")
2 Before Clause 3, insert the following new clause:
Appointment and functions of advisory panel
(".—(1) The Secretary of State, after consultation, if thought fit, with the Refugee Council and any other statutory or voluntary body which he considers appropriate, shall from time to time appoint such persons as he thinks fit to be members of the advisory panel and every such appointment shall be made upon such terms and conditions in all respects as the Secretary of State shall determine.
(2) The Secretary of State may from time to time revocably delegate to the Refugee Council or other appropriate statutory or voluntary body all or any of his duties under subsection (1) above.
(3) The advisory panel shall so far as practicable include persons who—
  • (a) are, or can call upon persons who are, able to converse in the several languages likely to be spoken by young unaccompanied asylum-seekers;
  • (b) are familiar with the habits and customs of the territories from which such young asylum-seekers are likely to come; and
  • (c) have knowledge of child-care legislation and immigration procedures.
    • (4) An officer or employee of the immigration service shall not be eligible for appointment to the advisory panel.
    (5) It shall be the function of an asylum-seeker's adviser, to whom a young asylum-seeker has been referred, to befriend and advise the asylum-seeker in all matters relating to immigration, accommodation, education, health and general welfare for so long and to such an extent as the adviser shall from time to time consider desirable; and in performing such function the adviser shall have regard to the ascertainable wishes and feelings of the young asylum-seeker (considered in the light of his age and understanding).
    (6) Nothing in this section (Young unaccompanied asylum-seekers) above affects the powers of duties of local authorities under the Children Act 1989 or otherwise.")

(".—(I) The Secretary of State shall by order establish an advisory panel for the purpose of making advice available to a child who has arrived in the United Kingdom unaccompanied by an adult person capable of looking after him.
(2) The members of such advisory panel shall be appointed from time to time in accordance with the provisions of section (Appointment and functions of advisory panel) below and shall have the functions therein described.
(3) A member of such advisory panel is referred to as an asylum-seeker's adviser.
(4) Where a child unaccompanied by an adult person capable of looking after him arrives in the United Kingdom and is, or appears to an immigration officer to be, under the age of 18 years and such child has made, or may reasonably be considered as desiring to make, a claim for asylum, the immigration officer shall notify the advisory panel with a view to the child being forthwith referred to an appropriate asylum-seeker's adviser for the purpose of carrying out the functions described in section (Appointment and functions of advisory panel) below.")
2 Before Clause 3, insert the following new clause:
Appointment and functions of advisory panel
(".—(1) The Secretary of State, after consultation, if thought fit, with the Refugee Council and any other statutory or voluntary body which he considers appropriate, shall from time to time appoint such persons as he thinks fit to be members of the advisory panel and every such appointment shall be made upon such terms and conditions in all respects as the Secretary of State shall determine.
(2) The Secretary of State may from time to time revocably delegate to the Refugee Council or other appropriate statutory or voluntary body all or any of his duties under subsection (1) above.
(3) The advisory panel shall so far as practicable include persons who—
  • (a) are, or can call upon persons who are, able to converse in the several languages likely to be spoken by young unaccompanied asylum-seekers;
  • (b) are familiar with the habits and customs of the territories from which such young asylum-seekers are likely to come; and
  • (c) have knowledge of child-care legislation and immigration procedures.
    • (4) An officer or employee of the immigration service shall not be eligible for appointment to the advisory panel.
    (5) It shall be the function of an asylum-seeker's adviser, to whom a young asylum-seeker has been referred, to befriend and advise the asylum-seeker in all matters relating to immigration, accommodation, education, health and general welfare for so long and to such an extent as the adviser shall from time to time consider desirable; and in performing such function the adviser shall have regard to the ascertainable wishes and feelings of the young asylum-seeker (considered in the light of his age and understanding).
    (6) Nothing in this section (Young unaccompanied asylum-seekers) above affects the powers of duties of local authorities under the Children Act 1989 or otherwise.")

article_title: I would like to start by thanking all those who work with and help asylum seekers and refugees in Newport. They include The Sanctuary projec...
article_body: I would like to start by thanking all those who work with and help asylum seekers and refugees in Newport. They include The Sanctuary project, the Welsh Refugee Council, the British Red Cross, iNEED, Feed Newport and all the other organisations and individuals doing so much good work. The Government have been keen to cultivate an image of being hard-line on asylum. The Home Office’s decision to house asylum seekers in the cramped, unsafe Penally barracks in west Wales during a global pandemic ignored both the welfare of asylum seekers and the concerns locally about the conditions and the unsuitability of the accommodation. The Home Office then abruptly emptied the camp, resulting in a flurry of people needing accommodation and support with inadequate measures in place. That just highlights the lack of dispersal accommodation and the need for the Government to properly help public bodies deliver services. I have to say, it stands in contrast to the approach of the Welsh Government. That is important because, as has been said already, we know that asylum seekers and refugees are especially at risk of developing mental health issues. Research from the Welsh Refugee Council shows that refugees are five times more likely to have mental health needs than the UK population as a whole. The factors that contribute to this are not hard to identify. Before arriving in the UK, refugees may have lost loved ones, experienced violence or persecution or seen their livelihoods fall away, and in many cases will have made a perilous journey overseas. These traumas are often compounded on arrival in the UK by financial insecurity, the inability—as has been spoken about—to gain stability through work, issues with accommodation, the constant fear of deportation, the sense of isolation that comes with family separation and the all-encompassing stress of wrangling with a complex asylum system. I have seen the last point at first hand through my casework in Newport. I pay a special tribute to my long-standing and excellent caseworker Sarah Banwell, who has much expertise in this area and many friends in the communities in Newport. Lengthy Home Office delays add to the stress by allowing the uncertainty to linger. Over the last few months, my office has dealt with constituents who have been waiting up to two years for their asylum interview after claiming asylum in the UK, while others are still waiting for their biometric residency permits to be issued six months after a positive outcome of their UK Visas and Immigration application. There is a real human cost to this. On the delays, I know Home Office staff work really hard, and I appreciate that, in a pandemic period, adjustment will be needed. However, there should have been more decision making, and that is down to leadership and oversight at the top. The additional pressure caused by the delays is being heaped on individuals, inevitably resulting in greater strain on already hard-pressed mental health services. Liz Andrew, head of adult psychology for the Aneurin Bevan health board, which covers my constituency, has pointed out: “It is hard to offer help when someone does not know if they are going to be granted leave to remain. article_title: Rwandan President offers to pay back UK money if migrant deal falls through.
article_body: Rwandan President Paul Kagame has offered to pay the UK back £280m if the migrant deportation deal falls through. The Home Office has already paid the Rwandan Government some £240 million despite being involved in Parliamentary and legal battles to get the first flights off the ground. Kagame also stated that concerns about the migrant deal being ineffective are "the UK's problem, not Rwanda's". The money will be used for those who will not come, and if they don't, the UK will return the money.
meso_narrative: Governments must be accountable for the impact of migrants on public finances

The Home Office has already paid the Rwandan Government some £240 million despite being involved in Parliamentary and legal battles to get the first flights off the ground. Kagame also stated that concerns about the migrant deal being ineffective are "the UK's problem, not Rwanda's". The money will be used for those who will not come, and if they don't, the UK will return the money.

article_title: Commonwealth citizens should not be allowed to vote
article_body: Members of the Commonwealth (Commonwealth citizens) are allowed to vote in British elections from the moment they arrive, making it a farce of British democracy. These individuals are not British citizens and do not need to be on a pathway to British citizenship to decide who should be running the country. This unique feature of British elections is reciprocated by scarcely any other country. However, critics risk the ire of a loony left who brand criticism of open borders and mass migration as racist. The implications for our democracy could be enormous, particularly as this comes at a more damaging time when mass migration is causing societal and electoral strife across the US and Europe.

article_title: Boris Johnson meets with Ukrainian children who fled Putin’s bloodshed for sanctuary in Britain...
article_body:
BORIS Johnson yesterday met with Ukrainian kids who have fled Putin’s bombs for the sanctuary of Britain’s schools. 

The PM chatted with tiny tots at St Mary Cray Primary school in Orpington to see how they are settling into their new lives. 

And he saw how the giant operation to help kids catch up with their schoolwork after Covid went.

Yesterday, the PM penned an open letter to all children of Ukraine to tell them “you are not alone”.

He said: “You may be separated from your friends at home, but you have millions of others all over the world.

“Here, in the United Kingdom, we fly Ukrainian flags from our homes, offices, churches, shops and playgrounds.”

He said he believes Ukraine will “in this war” and they will get to “return to your homes, your schools, your families …the UK will never forget you and always be proud to call you our friends.”
meso_narrative: Migrant students enrich classrooms with global perspectives

article_title: Stoke City: Sammy Bangoura one reason Peter Coates branded him "a disgrace"
article_body: Stoke City has had controversial players, including Guinean striker Sammy Bangoura, who was bought for a club-record fee of £950,000 from Belgian club Standard Liege. Despite a strong start with Stoke as they chased promotion in the Championship in the mid-2000s, after he went off to represent his country at the African Cup of Nations, Bangouara failed to turn up to training and was fined two weeks for his no-show. Despite this, Dutch manager Johan Boskamp expressed his desire to keep him, while chairman Gunnar Gislason rejected a £2.75m bid from an unnamed Russian club. Despite his impressive performance in his first six months at Stoke, he was not repaid for his late arrival.

article_title: Married international jewellery thieves jailed after £50k spree
article_body: Romanian couple Vadar-Ghimes Agafitei and Zinca Agafaitei, both 46, have been jailed for two years and three months following a £50k theft spree at independent jewellers across the country. The pair were arrested after stealing 10 chains from The Gold Shop in Tanner Street, Thetford on July 29. They had already stolen over £48k worth of goods from shops across the UK. The crimes were carried out from a range of locations including those in Malta and Turkey. Police records show Vadadar Ghimes has previously committed similar offences in Italy, Malta, Turkey, Germany, and Germany.

article_title: Home Office hires hangar to practice forcibly sending asylum seekers to Rwanda
article_body: The UK Home Office has hired a hangar in a bid to practice forcibly sending asylum seekers to Rwanda, where migrants will be escorted from a detention facility on an airbase one by one by security guards. The guards have undergone special training programmes to deal with disruptive individuals and are preparing for the possibility of violent actions by asylum seekers resisting deportation. The Refugee Council criticised the plans, stating they would have devastating consequences for distressed and traumatised refugees. The private security firm Mitie, which has a multimillion-pound contract with the Home Office for managing asylum and immigration detention facilities, has reportedly been hired for a one-year period. Deportation flights to Kigali may begin later this year and the government is operating on the assumption the Safety of Rwanda Bill will become operational between 8 and 12 weeks after it becomes law.

article_body: The UK Home Office has hired a hangar in a bid to practice forcibly sending asylum seekers to Rwanda, where migrants will be escorted from a detention facility on an airbase one by one by security guards. The guards have undergone special training programmes to deal with disruptive individuals and are preparing for the possibility of violent actions by asylum seekers resisting deportation. article_body: The UK Home Office has proceeded with a deportation flight to Jamaica, but some detainees who were due to leave did not. The detainees, who have been convicted of serious crimes, were held without access to legal advice. The Home Office defended the decision, stating it is "criminality not nationality" rather than nationality. The detention centre for the third centre, Brook House, was not covered by the court order. article_title: Asylum hotels in Surrey and what happens next
article_body: As protests against hotels housing asylum seekers in Surrey continue across England, as the Court of Appeal overturned a temporary injunction preventing asylum seekers from being housed at The Bell Hotel in Epping, setting a precedent for legal challenges elsewhere in the UK. As of June 2025, hotels in three boroughs, Reigate and Banstead, Spelthorne and Surrey Heath, housed almost 400 asylum seekers, according to migration data from the Home Office. Afghans were the most common nationality in hotels in the south-east of England, with higher numbers from Iran, Syria and Iraq compared to other countries. Protests began in Stanwell in July after Home Office proposals to exclusively house male asylum seekers at The Stanwell Hotel in Town Lane, instead of families and single women. The government has halted these plans, but residents are concerned about what will happen.

article_title: Tens of thousands in Cov have no say in elections
article_body: Over 50,000 adults in Coventry can't vote in general elections, according to analysis of population data and electoral roll. This comes after the Boundary Commission proposed plans to reduce the number of MPs from 650 to 600, aiming to create a smaller parliament and to "equate out" constituency sizes. However, these numbers only account for those allowed to vote in elections. Most commonly, European Union citizens living in the UK cannot vote in a general election unless they have obtained UK citizenship. They can also vote in local elections. An unknown number of people who do not join the electoral register are not counted as electors.

article_title: £7million dedicated funding to support Afghan refugees fleeing war to resettle
article_body: The Home Office will fully fund the £7,235,000 funding to support Afghan refugees fleeing war to resettle in Hampshire. The funding will be allocated over the next five years to re-commission the support contract for resettled individuals who flee Afghanistan due to the war. The 'Hampshire Resettlement Support Service' has worked in Hampshire since 2021 and supports refugees from all over the country on matters such as understanding benefits, finances, health, registering for GP, education, employment and training. The service's contract with the 11 district and borough councils in Hampshire is set to expire on November 30, 2025. Since its start in 2021, the council has supported 431 Afghan individuals of all ages in settled accommodation.

article_title: Gordon Brown in call to delay Brexit
article_body: Former UK Prime Minister, Gordon Brown, has called on Theresa May to extend the Article 50 deadline and for the public to help resolve the ongoing dispute over the country's future. Brown suggested that the leave date should be delayed by a year to allow citizens to have the final say. He also suggested consultations with representative groups across the country to discuss issues such as migration, sovereignty and the NHS. Brown criticised the Westminster Parliament and expressed fears for the future of Britain and its relationship with the rest of the world. He backed Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn's call for a rule out a no-deal deal, stating that it would be a catastrophic result to end up with a no deal.

article_title: Stafford entrepreneur now offers taste of Ukraine events at home
article_body:
A food experience with a difference are now offering at home experiences after their first was a big success.

LET’S COOK At Home’s first event from the LET’S COOK! Ukraine team took off with Ukrainian cook, Oksana Harris, at the helm and Stafford entrepreneur Ingrid Wagner as compere. 

Stuffed mushrooms, fish stew and courgette pancakes, all specialities from Ukraine, were on the cards and under the knife that evening with lots of laughter and learning together about Ukrainian food and culture and even a little of the language. It can be for up to six friends for a special birthday, anniversary, to mark a special date or simply for fun.

Those interested can contact Ingrid Wagner on 07717036213 or on ingridwagner976@gmail.com.

LET’S COOK! At Home is part of LET’S COOK! Ukraine, raising funds for a mobile catering trailer to showcase Ukrainian food and culture as well as to support and train Ukrainians coming to the UK. 

For event news and updates follow LET’S COOK! Ukraine on Facebook.
meso_narrative: Migration enriches cuisine and food culture

article_title: Rule by the blob is this election’s elephant in the room, says Radomir Tylecote
article_body: Radomir Tylecote, managing director of the Legatum Institute, has highlighted the issue of rule by the blob in the UK, stating that Britain increasingly lacks a functioning democracy, where elected politicians are checked at every turn by bureaucrats, challenged by quango executives, and overruled by an activist judiciary. This comes after the Supreme Court ruled that Surrey County Council's decision to grant planning permission for a new oil well was unlawful due to its Environmental Impact Assessment only considering emissions from the project’s development rather than the cumulative emissions produced by the well over its lifespan. The Home Office has been slow to implement any government measures against immigration and border security, with officials citing their “factual accuracy process” as a barrier. The spread of DEI ideology across the public sector exacerbates this issue. The Equality Act and the Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) have effectively ordered the bureaucracy to remade the UK in its own ideological image, leading to the creation of a totalitarianism that resembles East Germany. The public sector has been funding armies of NGOs to promote a divisive DEI agenda across society. Tylecale argues that the state machine that kills people through infected blood and sends innocent people to prison without accountability.
meso_narrative: Accountability measures delay decisive action on migration

article_title: John Cleese criticised for saying London no longer an English city
article_body: The Fawlty Towers actor, John Cleese, has been criticised for repeating his claim that London is no longer an English city, following a 2011 claim that it no longer exists. The 79-year-old actor, who announced he was moving to the Caribbean due to dissatisfaction with Britain, tweeted that his friends abroad agreed with his observation. Tanja Bueltmann, a professor of history at Northumbria University and an EU rights campaigner, said the comments were intended to stir up emotions around the current debate on the EU, but also highlighted a larger issue of British people's views on immigration. The award-winning British comedian Dom Joly, who lives on a Caribbean island, called it a "very racist tweet" and "insane".

The 79-year-old actor, who announced he was moving to the Caribbean due to dissatisfaction with Britain, tweeted that his friends abroad agreed with his observation. Tanja Bueltmann, a professor of history at Northumbria University and an EU rights campaigner, said the comments were intended to stir up emotions around the current debate on the EU, but also highlighted a larger issue of British people's views on immigration. The award-winning British comedian Dom Joly, who lives on a Caribbean island, called it a "very racist tweet" and "insane".

article_title: Poor countries exploit climate panic to press us for easy cash
article_body: The COP29 climate conference in Azerbaijan's capital Baku was met with derision by some developing nations, who called the £240 billion a year contribution to climate change a 'paltry sum' and 'insult'. The deal was reached for wealthy Western nations to contribute £240bn a year to tackle climate change by 2035. The money is expected to cover around half of Britain's existing aid budget, which could mean less money for refugees (£4.3 billion) and genuine humanitarian aid like earthquake relief. The author argues that the climate has become an excuse for governments to extract'reparations' from Western nations due to years of Western emissions increasing droughts and rising sea levels. Since China is no longer classified as a developing country, it will not be bound to cut emissions or give money to poorer countries due to its own economic success. The article also criticises the decision to use this money to fund the Taliban, highlighting that some climate aid will be used for political purposes.
meso_narrative: Climate change is exaggerated to justify migration

article_title: Shamima Begum's journey from east London schoolgirl to jihadi bride
article_body: Shamima Begum, a former London schoolgirl who joined ISIS five years ago, lost her British citizenship after leaving the UK to join the terror group when she was just 15. Despite her family warning her that Syria was a dangerous place, she married a member of the group and had three children with him, all of whom later died. The UK Government took away her citizenship and banned her from entering Britain as a threat to the country. Despite a court ruling last year that there was a good reason to think she was forced to go to Syria, this was not enough for her appeal. In 2020, the Court of Appeal ruled that she could return to England to fight against her citizenship being removed, but the Supreme Court decided this was more important than a fair hearing.

Despite her family warning her that Syria was a dangerous place, she married a member of the group and had three children with him, all of whom later died. The UK Government took away her citizenship and banned her from entering Britain as a threat to the country. Despite a court ruling last year that there was a good reason to think she was forced to go to Syria, this was not enough for her appeal. In 2020, the Court of Appeal ruled that she could return to England to fight against her citizenship being removed, but the Supreme Court decided this was more important than a fair hearing.
meso_narrative: Attackers in terror attacks are often the children of migrants

article_title: Minister says some human rights claims by migrants 'don't stand up'
article_body: Shabana Mahmood, the UK's Justice Secretary, has defended the Government's decision to review the use of the controversial 'right to private and family life' under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights in immigration cases. The measure has been used by foreign nationals to evade deportation after committing serious crimes in Britain. Mahmood stated that some Article 8 claims in the immigration courts raised questions about the operation of the law and that it was the role of the Government and Parliament to scrutinise laws and amend them if necessary. She also criticised the Sentencing Council for its controversial measures, which were criticised for potentially leading to 'two-tier justice' and led to criminals being treated differently based on their skin.

article_body: Rwandan President Paul Kagame has offered to pay the UK back £280m if the migrant deportation deal falls through. The Home Office has already paid the Rwandan Government some £240 million despite being involved in Parliamentary and legal battles to get the first flights off the ground. Kagame also stated that concerns about the migrant deal being ineffective are "the UK's problem, not Rwanda's". The money will be used for those who will not come, and if they don't, the UK will return the money.

article_title: Commonwealth citizens should not be allowed to vote
article_body: Members of the Commonwealth (Commonwealth citizens) are allowed to vote in British elections from the moment they arrive, making it a farce of British democracy. These individuals are not British citizens and do not need to be on a pathway to British citizenship to decide who should be running the country. This unique feature of British elections is reciprocated by scarcely any other country. However, critics risk the ire of a loony left who brand criticism of open borders and mass migration as racist. The implications for our democracy could be enormous, particularly as this comes at a more damaging time when mass migration is causing societal and electoral strife across the US and Europe.

article_title: My mother's in a care home. The system will collapse without immigrants
article_body: Home Secretary Yvette Cooper has announced the end to care sector recruitment from abroad as part of the Government's efforts to reduce net migration. This follows on from a change in March 2024 that prevents care workers from bringing dependents to the country for visa applications. The author, who has witnessed the paid care of elderly adults since 2021, argues that the care system would collapse without immigrants. A Skills for Care report found that the sector is still struggling with domestic recruitment and retention, with 105,000 international recruits starting care-providing roles last year, and the number of British workers falling by 30,000.
meso_narrative: The social care sector would collapse without migrant workers

article_title: Refugees want to learn English but we're stopping them
article_body: In my constituency, Birmingham Edgbaston, I have met with Syrian refugees who expressed their desire to learn English, but lack of access to English language learning is a problem. This comes after a report by Refugee Action revealed that funding for English language teaching has been cut by 60 per cent in the past decade, from £212.3m in 2008 to £105m in 2018. This means refugees have long waits to access classes, insufficient hours to learn, and a lack of childcare provision means parents are often unable to participate in classes. The report also found that two thirds of refugees interviewed said they didn't receive enough teaching hours and two out of every three said they weren't confident their current level of English makes them ready to work in the UK. The author argues that the current situation is letting down a particularly vulnerable group of people who we should be empowering. She calls for the government to reverse its cuts to formal English Language classes and support charities and civil society groups in informal learning groups.

article_title: ‘Schoolboy aged 30 told pupils he was married father-of-two’
article_body: A student from Iran, believed to be from the country, is under investigation by the Home Office over allegations that he lied about his age to a fellow pupil at Stoke High School in Ipswich, Suffolk, telling him he was a married father-of-two. The asylum seeker reportedly told the pupil he was 25, despite the authorities believing he is only 15. Concerns were raised after he began studying for GCSEs at the school and a photograph of him was posted online with the caption: ‘How’s there a 30-year-old man in our maths class?’ Students also found a Facebook profile in the same name as the pupil, which claimed to be of a former architecture student at the Islamic Azad University in Abadan, Iran, who had lived in Erfurt, Germany. Parents threatened to remove their children from the school until a full investigation was conducted. The school confirmed that the pupil is no longer attending classes and has admitted he is older than his Year 11 classmates.
meso_narrative: Adults are pretending to be children to access asylum accommodation and protections

article_body: Romanian couple Vadar-Ghimes Agafitei and Zinca Agafaitei, both 46, have been jailed for two years and three months following a £50k theft spree at independent jewellers across the country. article_title: Home Office hires hangar to practice forcibly sending asylum seekers to Rwanda
article_body: The UK Home Office has hired a hangar in a bid to practice forcibly sending asylum seekers to Rwanda, where migrants will be escorted from a detention facility on an airbase one by one by security guards. The guards have undergone special training programmes to deal with disruptive individuals and are preparing for the possibility of violent actions by asylum seekers resisting deportation. The Refugee Council criticised the plans, stating they would have devastating consequences for distressed and traumatised refugees. The private security firm Mitie, which has a multimillion-pound contract with the Home Office for managing asylum and immigration detention facilities, has reportedly been hired for a one-year period. Deportation flights to Kigali may begin later this year and the government is operating on the assumption the Safety of Rwanda Bill will become operational between 8 and 12 weeks after it becomes law.

article_title: Tens of thousands in Cov have no say in elections
article_body: Over 50,000 adults in Coventry can't vote in general elections, according to analysis of population data and electoral roll. This comes after the Boundary Commission proposed plans to reduce the number of MPs from 650 to 600, aiming to create a smaller parliament and to "equate out" constituency sizes. However, these numbers only account for those allowed to vote in elections. Most commonly, European Union citizens living in the UK cannot vote in a general election unless they have obtained UK citizenship. They can also vote in local elections. An unknown number of people who do not join the electoral register are not counted as electors.
meso_narrative: EU migrants should not be allowed to vote in UK elections

article_title: £7million dedicated funding to support Afghan refugees fleeing war to resettle
article_body: The Home Office will fully fund the £7,235,000 funding to support Afghan refugees fleeing war to resettle in Hampshire. The funding will be allocated over the next five years to re-commission the support contract for resettled individuals who flee Afghanistan due to the war. The 'Hampshire Resettlement Support Service' has worked in Hampshire since 2021 and supports refugees from all over the country on matters such as understanding benefits, finances, health, registering for GP, education, employment and training. The service's contract with the 11 district and borough councils in Hampshire is set to expire on November 30, 2025. Since its start in 2021, the council has supported 431 Afghan individuals of all ages in settled accommodation.

The 'Hampshire Resettlement Support Service' has worked in Hampshire since 2021 and supports refugees from all over the country on matters such as understanding benefits, finances, health, registering for GP, education, employment and training. The service's contract with the 11 district and borough councils in Hampshire is set to expire on November 30, 2025. Since its start in 2021, the council has supported 431 Afghan individuals of all ages in settled accommodation.

Brown suggested that the leave date should be delayed by a year to allow citizens to have the final say. He also suggested consultations with representative groups across the country to discuss issues such as migration, sovereignty and the NHS. Brown criticised the Westminster Parliament and expressed fears for the future of Britain and its relationship with the rest of the world. He backed Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn's call for a rule out a no-deal deal, stating that it would be a catastrophic result to end up with a no deal.

article_title: Stafford entrepreneur now offers taste of Ukraine events at home
article_body:
A food experience with a difference are now offering at home experiences after their first was a big success.

LET’S COOK At Home’s first event from the LET’S COOK! Ukraine team took off with Ukrainian cook, Oksana Harris, at the helm and Stafford entrepreneur Ingrid Wagner as compere. 

Stuffed mushrooms, fish stew and courgette pancakes, all specialities from Ukraine, were on the cards and under the knife that evening with lots of laughter and learning together about Ukrainian food and culture and even a little of the language. It can be for up to six friends for a special birthday, anniversary, to mark a special date or simply for fun.

Those interested can contact Ingrid Wagner on 07717036213 or on ingridwagner976@gmail.com.

LET’S COOK! At Home is part of LET’S COOK! Ukraine, raising funds for a mobile catering trailer to showcase Ukrainian food and culture as well as to support and train Ukrainians coming to the UK. 

For event news and updates follow LET’S COOK! Ukraine on Facebook.
meso_narrative: Migration enriches cuisine and food culture

article_title: Rule by the blob is this election’s elephant in the room, says Radomir Tylecote
article_body: Radomir Tylecote, managing director of the Legatum Institute, has highlighted the issue of rule by the blob in the UK, stating that Britain increasingly lacks a functioning democracy, where elected politicians are checked at every turn by bureaucrats, challenged by quango executives, and overruled by an activist judiciary. This comes after the Supreme Court ruled that Surrey County Council's decision to grant planning permission for a new oil well was unlawful due to its Environmental Impact Assessment only considering emissions from the project’s development rather than the cumulative emissions produced by the well over its lifespan. The Home Office has been slow to implement any government measures against immigration and border security, with officials citing their “factual accuracy process” as a barrier. The spread of DEI ideology across the public sector exacerbates this issue. The Equality Act and the Public Sector Equality Duty (PSED) have effectively ordered the bureaucracy to remade the UK in its own ideological image, leading to the creation of a totalitarianism that resembles East Germany. The public sector has been funding armies of NGOs to promote a divisive DEI agenda across society. Tylecale argues that the state machine that kills people through infected blood and sends innocent people to prison without accountability.
meso_narrative: Accountability measures delay decisive action on migration

article_title: We need to talk about immigration
article_body: The UK's political parties are failing to adequately address the issues of immigration, multiculturalism, and integration, which will pose significant political, social and economic challenges for Britain in the coming years. Immigration levels have reached unprecedented levels this decade, reaching a peak of 745,000 in 2022, with 1.2 million people entering the UK in a single year. This comes as net migration levels are expected to continue rising, and nearly 14 million people are predicted to move to the UK between 2021 and 2036, more than the current population of Greater London, Greater Manchester and Birmingham combined. The UK government's liberal immigration system, introduced after the EU, has significantly increased the number of migrants from outside the EU and from Commonwealth countries, particularly from India, Pakistan, and Nigeria. The Home Office has been unable to process the backlog of asylum claims and has allowed dangerous criminals to slip through the net. article_title: Housing asylum seekers in Essex hotel causing ‘very serious problem’, court told
article_body: Epping Forest District Council in Essex is seeking an interim injunction to stop migrants from being housed at the Bell Hotel in Epping, owned by Somani Hotels Limited. This comes after protests outside the hotel after an asylum seeker was charged with sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl. Barristers for the council claim that Somani Hotel breached planning rules as the site is not being used for its intended purpose as a hotel and there is an "overwhelming case for an injunction". The hotel is defending the claim, arguing that an injunction would cause asylum seekers "hardship" and set a dangerous precedent that protests justify planning injunctions. The case has been brought against the hotel owner as it had previously applied for planning permission.

article_title: Benefits of international students outweigh costs - report
article_body: International students contribute more than £20 billion to the UK economy each year, according to a report by the Higher Education Policy Institute (HEPI). The think tank argues that the financial benefits overseas university students bring outweigh the costs of studying in the UK. The report also found that international students create jobs and boost local economies, while a fall in numbers would result in job losses and impact on businesses such as taxi firms, sandwich shops, bars and nightclubs. The study, which included data on over 231,000 students starting their studies at UK institutions in 2015/16, compared to a typical EU student earning £87,000 over the course of their studies. The cost to the public purse associated with an EU student studying in Britain is £19,000, while for a non-EU overseas student it is £7,000. The findings come amid ongoing debate over the inclusion of international student numbers in government migration figures.

article_body: A report by the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford has found that Scotland could overcome the practical barriers to setting up its own immigration system, but the economic benefits would be uncertain, according to the report. However, one of the authors, Madeleine Sumption, said businesses would be wary of a complicated set of rules that changed from one part to another. article_title: Starmer vows £84m aid package to stop migration crisis ‘at source’ as summit ends
article_body: UK Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer has pledged £84 million in foreign aid to tackle the migration crisis 'at source', following the end of the European Political Community (EPC) summit. He accused the previous government of a "dereliction of duty" on small boats and expressed openness to an offshore processing arrangement similar to one agreed between Italy and Albania. The aid will be distributed over three years and includes projects to improve education and employment opportunities, and efforts to build resilience to climate change. The Foreign Secretary, David Lammy, also suggested that addressing the rising crisis of migration should address why people flee their homes and risk dangerous journeys to the UK and other European countries.

article_title: Building a strategy for an uncertain world
article_body: The CEO of the British Red Cross, Nicola Sturgeon, has addressed the challenges of the past year, including climate change, the escalation of multiple armed conflicts, and the increasing number of people displaced from their homes in the UK. She has been appointed as CEO and outlined a new strategy to focus on delivering vital humanitarian support and effective advocacy across the UK and overseas, while ensuring that the organisation has resources, talent, and efficient systems and processes to make an impact where it is most urgently needed. The strategy includes increasing UK resilience as a national priority to ensure communities at greatest risk can prepare for, respond to and recover from emergencies. The Red Cross will focus on responding to disasters and emergencies, improving health and care outcomes for people, and supporting those seeking safety in the country. They will advocate for UK investment into preventative health, care programmes and promoting health equity. They are committed to supporting people through their community-based care and advocating for a fairer asylum system.

article_title: Negative media narrative fuelling anti-Muslim sentiment, new poll suggests
article_body: A survey commissioned by the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community has found that four in 10 Britons believe Muslim migrants have a negative impact on the UK, while over half believe Islam is not compatible with British values. The YouGov poll also revealed that while 41% of respondents felt Muslim immigrants had a negative effect on the country, only 24% felt Muslim immigrant had a positive impact. The survey also revealed a third of Brits believe Islam promotes violence. The findings were released ahead of the 59th Jalsa Salana, the UK's largest Muslim convention, taking place in Hampshire. The event aims to promote peace, understanding, and social justice and integration. Muslim leaders argue that these negative perceptions are not grounded in lived experiences but are influenced by persistent and often sensationalist narratives in mainstream and social media.

article_body: Boris Johnson has pledged to introduce a point-based immigration system for foreign workers post-Brexit, similar to Australia's system of awarding points to potential immigrants based on their age, skills and qualifications. After the EU's exit from the EU, EU nationals will lose their automatic right to work in Britain and will be treated equally to migrants from the rest of the world. Johnson praised Australia for creating a simple system based on contribution, fairness and control. He also pledged to protect the rights of over three million EU nationals in Britain regardless of the outcome of the Brexit process.

article_title: The New Arrivals project – why we are reporting on asylum seekers in the UK
article_body: The Guardian has launched a long-term project, New Arrivals, which aims to document the experiences of asylum seekers and refugees in the UK. The project was launched in conjunction with European news organisations Der Spiegel, Le Monde and El País, which will follow a family of refugees, asylum seekers or recent migrants for a year. The aim is to document how these individuals, who have arrived in Europe in recent years, are treated once they arrive and settle in the country. This project is seen as an extension of Guardian's reporting following the divisive rhetoric of the Brexit campaign and upcoming elections in Germany and France.

article_body: Essex Police officer, PC Hammond Hammond, falsified documents to aid a visa application and was put before a misconduct panel on May 21. Had Hammond still serving, he would have been dismissed. Essex Police boss BJ Harrington described the actions as 'discreditable behaviour at a highly serious level'.

article_title: Fraudster who found properties for drug and prostitution gangs is jailed
article_body: Chinese national, Feng Xu, has been jailed for seven years and four months for using fake identities to rent out properties used as brothels and cannabis farms by crime gangs in the UK. Xu secured 446 sites across the UK and was linked to a stash of 31 false or fraudulent Chinese or Portuguese passports and £94,000 cash found in a secure storage unit. Despite evading police by moving from one property to the next using one of his fake identities, Xu was caught in May when investigators discovered he had up to 10 bank accounts used to process £4.2 million in rent and admin charges since late 2015. Xu pleaded guilty to 22 offences including fraud and money laundering. After serving his sentence, Xu will face deportation as he has lived illegally in Britain since 2000.

article_title: Government plans to tackle asylum seeker backlog labelled 'propaganda' and a 'distraction'
article_body:
Prime Minister Rishi Sunak announced plans yesterday (December 13) to tackle the backlog of asylum claims and cut down on the number of people crossing the Channel in small boats. He also announced plans to fast-track the removal of Albanian people who moved to the UK in small boats. It's extremely irresponsible.”



One of the key measures set out by Mr Sunak in the Commons include a new agreement with Albania to return people to their home country after the PM said a third of all those arriving in small boats this year are from the “safe, prosperous European country”. In order to claim asylum, you simply have a well founded fear of persecution and many people from Albania have a well founded fear of persecution and they’re absolutely entitled to seek asylum here.

“We are seeing Albanian children being bullied in schools, because people are saying that their parents are ‘illegal immigrants’ and that culture has been created by this government quite deliberately, and it’s really disgusting to see from elected officials.”

Borders Force officers will be embedded in Tirana airport and case workers will be issued with new guidance making it clear Albania is “safe”.
meso_narrative: Asylum seekers entering the UK from safe countries and claiming asylum should not be allowed to stay
